q: The technician switches on the chartplotter, waits for the fix, shows you this and turns to the VHF. What do you ask before he moves on?
a: Whether the card covers the whole cruising ground, and how old the chart is
o: Nothing — a plotter with a fix is a working plotter
Whether the screen can be dimmed for night passages
Whether the plotter also drives the autopilot
why: Check the chart covers everywhere you will go and ask its edition: an old card misses new marinas, moles and shoals.

q: At the berth the instruments show this, and the base's harbour plan gives 3.0 m here. What has happened?
a: The sounder is set to feet — 9.8 ft is 3.0 m; switch the units to metres
o: The transducer is fouled — the reading is random
It shows the depth at the harbour mouth, not the berth
The offset is set below the keel — add the draught
why: 9.8 ft = 3.0 m. Greek and Croatian charts are in metres: set depth to metres and distance to nautical miles before you sail.

lines: Harbour plan: 3.0 m at the berth

q: You check the sounder against the harbour plan at the berth. How much water is under the keel right now?
a: About 1.6 m — the sounder reads from the transducer, not from the keel
o: 3.3 m — the reading is already the water below the keel
1.4 m — take the draught off the reading
3.5 m — the plan is right and the sounder is 0.2 m out
why: No offset: the reading is depth below the transducer, 0.2 m under the surface here. Below the keel: 3.5 − 1.9 ≈ 1.6 m.

lines: Harbour plan: 3.5 m at the berth

q: Going through the plotter, the technician points at the MOB key and moves on. What do you do with it?
a: Ask him to show how it marks and how it clears, then brief the crew on it
o: Leave it — a casualty is recovered by eye, not from a screen
Note that it is the red button on the VHF handset
Press and hold it now to test the DSC distress alert
why: MOB on the plotter drops a waypoint and shows bearing and distance back; the crew must know where it is before it is needed.

q: On the test run outside the harbour the display shows this. What do you write on the check-in form?
a: Log reads zero — paddle wheel fouled; ask the base to clear it
o: GPS fault — SOG shows a speed with no log input
Nothing — SOG from the plotter does for the week
Plotter has lost its fix — reboot it at the berth
why: A fouled paddle wheel reads 0; the base pulls and cleans it in the harbour. Note it: speed through the water feeds true wind and the log book.

q: A steady breeze blows across the marina and the burgee flies at the masthead, yet the instruments show this. What do you do?
a: Note it — masthead unit dead; ask the base to look at it before you leave
o: Accept it — the wind shows only once the boat is sailing
Go up in the bosun's chair and check the sensor yourself
Tap the display — it needs some minutes to warm up
why: The wind instrument should show direction and speed at the berth; a dead one is logged and fixed by the base, not by you aloft.

q: This is the whole of the technician's autopilot briefing. What do you do?
a: Ask to see Standby, a course change and the alarms, and try it on the test run
o: Accept it — AUTO is the only button you will need
Read the manual the first time you need it at sea
Leave it switched off and hand-steer for the week
why: Know how to engage, disengage and what the alarm means before you rely on it — and never in harbours or close quarters.

fig.title: Autopilot
lines: Not tried on the test run

q: The technician finishes his radio check and leaves the set like this. What do you set before leaving the berth?
a: Channel 16, dual watch on the base's working channel, squelch just above the hiss
o: Leave 72 — the base calls you on it all week
Channel 16 with squelch fully up to keep it quiet
Channel 16 alone — dual watch drains the battery
why: Under way you keep a watch on 16; dual watch adds the working channel. Squelch fully up mutes weak calls.

q: The technician asks you to do the radio check yourself. How do you make the call?
a: Call the base on its working channel with the boat's name and ask for a readability report
o: Call the base on channel 16 — a check must be heard by all
Send a DSC test call to the base on channel 70
Call the coastguard on channel 16 and ask for a check
why: Radio checks go on a working channel, not on 16, which is kept for distress, safety and calling.

q: You open the DSC page of the fixed VHF and look at the front of the set. What do you do?
a: Ask for the boat's MMSI to be programmed and the cover replaced before you sign
o: Enter the MMSI printed on your own SRC certificate
Program the base's phone number in as the MMSI
Ignore it — DSC is for ships, not charter yachts
why: Without the ship's MMSI a DSC alert carries no identity; the cover prevents false alerts. Both are the base's job.

q: The inventory lists a handheld VHF. This is what you find in the chart-table drawer. What do you do?
a: Ask for the charger and a full charge before you sign, and note it on the form
o: Leave it — the fixed set is the one that matters
Take it as it is — one bar lasts a week on standby
Have it struck off the inventory to avoid a deposit claim
why: The handheld is the radio for the dinghy and the liferaft; flat and without a charger it is useless. Have it charged and listed.

q: The plotter's AIS page shows the harbour traffic. What do you ask the technician?
a: Whether it is receive-only or a transponder — can the ferries see you?
o: Whether it shows yachts as well as ships
Whether the targets also appear on the VHF screen
Whether the CPA alarm can be switched off at night
why: A receiver shows others to you; only a transponder shows you to them. Know which before you cross a ferry route at night.

q: On the test run, in flat water with no current, you compare the steering compass with the plotter's course over the ground. What do you do?
a: Look for a phone or speaker by the binnacle, then note the deviation that remains
o: Set the plotter to magnetic north so that the two agree
Accept 8° — that is the variation in the Ionian
Swing the compass yourself before leaving the harbour
why: Compass 090° + 3°E variation = 093° true; the other 5° is deviation — often a phone on the binnacle. Note it; the plotter steers by GPS.

q: You tick the navigation kit off against the inventory. What do you ask the base for?
a: A pilot book of the area and a current chart, before you sign
o: Nothing — the chartplotter replaces all of it
A second pair of binoculars for the crew
A tide table and a set of tidal-stream atlases
why: Paper chart and pilot book are the backup and the harbour detail the plotter lacks; an old chart misses new moles and depths.

q: In the chart-table drawer you find this. The technician says nobody uses it any more. What do you do with it during the week?
a: Keep it: each day's departure and arrival, positions and times, engine hours, weather, anything that broke
o: Leave it — the plotter's track is the boat's record
Fill it in on Friday evening from memory before the check-out
Use it only if the port police ask to see a log
why: The log is your record for the base, the insurer and the port police: when you were where, the engine hours, the damage you reported.

fig.title: Log book
lines: Columns: time, position, course, log, wind, engine hours
Pencil on a string, half the pages left

q: Your mate, who has no radio certificate, asks whether she may use the VHF during the week. What do you tell her?
a: Yes, under your supervision as the certificated operator — and anyone may call in distress
o: No — only the holder of the SRC may touch the set
Yes, freely — the boat's ship licence covers the crew
Only the handheld, never the fixed DSC set
why: The ship licence covers the set; an SRC holder is in charge of it and crew operate under supervision. Distress may be sent by anyone.
ref: VHF licence — operator and ship station

q: The base's briefing has a weather page. What do you take from it when you plan the week?
a: Sail early, reef before the afternoon, allow for the current in the channel
o: Ignore tide and current — there is none in the Med
Plan the long legs for the afternoon, when the wind is up
Stay in the marina on every day the Meltemi blows
why: The Med has little tide, but wind-driven currents in channels are real; the Meltemi builds by afternoon, so passages go early.

q: You switch the plotter on at the berth in the base and it shows this. What do you do?
a: Treat it as a stale fix — wait for a lock, then check the position against the berth
o: Enter a position correction so the boat sits on the berth
Assume the base moved the boat overnight
Accept it — plotters are good to about half a mile
why: Until it has satellites the plotter shows the last stored position. Check the fix time and that the boat sits on its berth before trusting it.
ref: Check-in: GPS fix at the berth

fig.note: Plotter screen at the berth, Sat 17:00

q: You set up the sounder's shallow-water alarm from these figures. What do you set it to?
a: About 3 m — the keel touches at 1.7 m on this sounder, plus a margin
o: 1.0 m as found — the alarm is about the hull, not the keel
2.1 m — the draught, exactly
5 m — anything closer is a nuisance in Greek bays
why: The keel touches when the sounder reads 2.1 − 0.4 = 1.7 m; add a metre or so of margin. Set it, and tell the crew what the alarm means.

q: The depth sounder is blank and the base answers as shown. What do you do?
a: Have it written on the form as unserviceable and ask for a fix or a lead line before you sail
o: Sail anyway — the Ionian is deep and you know the bays
Refuse the boat and demand the deposit back
Sign now and raise it by phone with the base on Monday
why: A dead instrument is noted at hand-over so it is not charged to you, and a boat without depth is not fit to anchor: push for a fix.

q: The plotter's display menu looks like this, and Tuesday's plan is to leave Kos at 03:00 for Astypalaia. What do you set up now, at the berth?
a: Find the night palette and the dimmer and try them, so that you can set them in the dark
o: Leave it at 100 % — the brighter the screen, the safer the night
Set AUTO and forget it — the plotter knows when it gets dark
Switch the plotter off at night and steer by the compass alone
why: At 100 % the screen kills your night vision; the night colours and the dimmer are found in daylight, not fumbled for at 03:00.

q: Reading the plotter again on Sunday morning, before the lines come off, you find this. What do you do?
a: Clear the active route and the old waypoints, then build your own from the chart
o: Follow it — the previous crew clearly knew the area
Keep it and mute the two alarms for the week
Delete everything, including the base's own harbour marks
why: A stranger's route steers you to their anchorages with their alarms; a plotter left clean shows only what you put in it.

fig.title: Plotter — routes
lines: XTE alarm: on · arrival alarm: 0.1 M

q: The contract allows the Turkish coast from Bodrum to Datça, and the plotter shows this. What do you do before you sign?
a: Ask the base for a card that covers Turkey, or paper charts of that coast — before you sign
o: Rely on the phone app — it streams the Turkish coast when you need it
Sail by the base map — the harbours over there are easy
Cross anyway — the AIS and the depth sounder will show the shoals
why: A base map has no depths or hazards; for every mile the contract lets you sail you need a chart, electronic or paper.
ref: Check-in: chart coverage vs cruising area

fig.title: Plotter — cartography
lines: Turkey coast: base map only, no depths

q: The technician calls the tablet in the chart table 'the backup plotter'. What do you check before it earns that name?
a: That the charts are downloaded for offline use and that it charges from the boat's 12 V
o: That it has a SIM card — the charts stream from the internet
That it shows AIS targets like the fixed plotter does
Nothing — a backup is only looked at when the plotter dies
why: A backup that needs a phone signal and a wall socket is no backup: offline charts of the whole area and a 12 V lead, checked now.

fig.title: Tablet
lines: Charger: USB lead, no 12 V plug

q: Your crew's navigator says she will do the week on her phone app and the paper chart is 'for the port police'. What do you tell her?
a: Fine as a third source — the plotter is the primary and the paper chart the backup
o: Fine — a modern app is more up to date than any plotter card
No — phones are banned from navigation on a charter boat
Fine, as long as she keeps it in a waterproof case at the helm
why: A phone overheats, goes flat and dies with the signal; its crowd-sourced depths are not surveyed. Use it, but not alone.

fig.title: Phone chart app
lines: Battery: 40 % · in the sun at the helm

q: Monday, 11:00, motoring north in the Kos–Kalymnos channel at cruising revs, the displays show this. What is happening?
a: Nearly 2 kn of current against you — the log is through the water, SOG over the ground
o: The log is over-reading — the paddle wheel needs calibrating
The GPS has a stale fix — SOG lags behind the real speed
The engine is losing power — check the fuel filter
why: STW is what the paddle wheel sees; SOG is what the ground sees. The difference is the current — the briefing warned of 2 kn here.
ref: SOG vs speed through the water

lines: Cruising revs, flat water, no wind

q: Sunday, at anchor in a bay you came into in daylight, your crew ask what the thin line behind the boat on the plotter is. What do you tell them?
a: The track — where the boat has been; it is your way back out in the dark
o: The route — where the plotter wants to take you next
The chart's depth contour — the boat sits on the 5 m line
The anchor circle — the plotter's drag alarm
why: The track records your positions; following it back out is the safest line in a bay you have already crossed.

q: Thursday's plan is a night passage across the Piraeus ferry route. You set the plotter up on Wednesday evening. What do you set?
a: A CPA alarm on AIS targets at a range that leaves time to act, and test that it sounds
o: Alarms off — they wake the off-watch for every fishing boat
CPA 0.1 M, so that only a real collision course sounds
Nothing — with a transponder the ferries will avoid you
why: A guard zone or CPA alarm is your second lookout at night; set it wide enough to act on and check that you can hear it from the helm.
ref: AIS — CPA alarm and guard zone

q: Monday, 09:30, weighing anchor in a crowded bay. The crew member at the wheel presses AUTO so that he can go forward and help. What do you do?
a: Take him off it and keep a hand on the wheel — nobody leaves the helm in a crowded anchorage
o: Let him — AUTO holds a heading better than a hand does
Let him, but set the heading at the gap between the boats
Have him use wind mode instead — it reacts faster to gusts
why: The autopilot steers a heading, not round boats and chains; in harbours and anchorages a person steers and the pilot stays on Standby.

q: Running home under main and genoa with a preventer rigged, the pilot is in wind mode. What happens when the wind veers 20° — and what do you do?
a: The pilot follows the wind 20° to starboard; check the new heading on the chart, then alter or change mode
o: Nothing changes — wind mode holds the course over the ground
The pilot gybes the boat — switch to compass mode at once
The pilot alarms and drops to Standby — hand-steer until it settles
why: Wind mode keeps the apparent wind angle, so it will not gybe you — but it steers where the wind goes; someone must watch the course.

q: On the test run the autopilot's heading agrees with neither the steering compass nor the plotter. The technician's answer is shown. What do you do?
a: Ask the base to do the calibration and the heading alignment now, in calm water, and check again
o: Do the circles yourself after leaving the harbour on Sunday
Ignore it — the pilot holds a course even if its number is wrong
Set the plotter's heading source to the pilot so that they agree
why: A pilot with an uncalibrated fluxgate steers badly, especially on turns; calibration is the base's job, done before the boat is signed for.

fig.title: Test run, headings
lines: Technician: “do a couple of circles, it learns”

q: The technician leaves the VHF on low power 'because the base is close'. Thursday you will be 20 miles offshore. What do you do with the setting?
a: 1 W in harbour for the base, 25 W for calling at sea — and a distress call always on 25 W
o: Leave 1 W all week — 25 W drains the batteries
Set 25 W now for everything — more power is always better
25 W only on channel 16; the working channels stay on 1 W
why: Low power keeps a harbour chat local; at sea and in distress you want the full 25 W. Know which key switches it before you need it.

fig.title: Fixed VHF
lines: Base: “leave it, we are 200 m away”

q: Sunday evening, stern-to in Fiskardo, the VHF chatters on 16 all evening and your crew want it off. What do you tell them?
a: In harbour it may go off or down; the watch on 16 is for when you are under way
o: It stays on 16 at full volume all week — that is the law
Switch it to the base's channel — they may call you
Leave it on 16 at the lowest volume so that nobody hears it
why: A listening watch on 16 is kept under way; alongside at night the set may be off or turned down — the harbour office has its own channel.

q: Tuesday, 15:00, at anchor off Vathi. You come below to the alarm and this screen; your seven-year-old is at the chart table. What do you do, in order?
a: Cancel on the set, then call the coastguard on 16: boat's name, MMSI, position, 'false alert, cancel'
o: Switch the set off — the alert stops when the power goes
Nothing — it was undesignated, so nobody will respond to it
Call the base on the working channel and ask them to cancel it
why: A DSC distress alert is live until cancelled by voice on 16; the coastguard needs your name, MMSI and position to stand down.
ref: DSC — cancelling a false distress alert

q: The technician does the radio check from the office 50 m away and gets 'loud and clear'. What does that tell you about the masthead antenna?
a: Little — at 50 m a broken antenna cable still gets through; ask for a check from a station miles away
o: Everything — if it reaches the office, it reaches the coastguard
That the antenna is at the masthead, so the range is 25 miles
That the set is on 25 W — on 1 W the office would not hear it
why: Range comes from the antenna and its cable; a check across the pontoon proves only that the set transmits. Call a station on the horizon.

fig.title: Radio check
lines: Antenna: masthead; deck plug taped up

q: At the helm the depth display is blank, while the one at the chart table shows the depth. What do you tell the base?
a: The helm display or its network plug has failed — the sounder is fine; fix it or note it on the form
o: The transducer is dead — a diver must look at the hull before you sail
Nothing — the chart-table display is enough for the week
Switch everything off and on again; it will come back by itself
why: One instrument reading at one display and not at another is the network, not the sensor: the connector at the helm is the usual culprit.

fig.title: Instruments
lines: Chart table: depth 3.4 m, wind 8 kn

q: Wednesday morning after a rolly night at anchor, the spare halyard has been slapping the mast and the wind display shows this in a flat calm. What do you do?
a: Look up — the halyard has likely fouled the masthead unit; free it from the deck, tell the base, sail by eye
o: Switch the instrument off — a reading like this means the electronics are failing
Reef now and keep it in — the instrument knows better than your eye
Stay put and call the base for a replacement unit before you move
why: A halyard wrapped on the masthead unit jams the cups or bends the vane; free it, tell the base, and sail without the number until it is fixed.

q: Sunday evening you motor-sail into the dusk with the main up and the engine on. Which switches go on?
a: NAV and STEAMING — sidelights, sternlight and the masthead steaming light
o: TRICOLOUR and STEAMING — the two brightest, at the top
TRICOLOUR alone — the sail is up, so you are a sailing vessel
NAV alone — the engine is only helping the sail
why: Engine on means power-driven: sidelights, sternlight and the steaming light (Rule 23). The tricolour is for sail alone.

q: Monday, 22:00, under sail alone, your crew set the panel like this 'to be seen'. What do you change?
a: Tricolour alone, or NAV alone — never both — and the deck light off; it blinds the helm
o: Add STEAMING as well — the more light, the better you are seen
Leave it — an extra light never hurt anyone at night
Add ANCHOR too, so that the ferries see a white light
why: Rule 25: a sailing vessel shows either the deck-level set or the tricolour, not both; a deck light hides your lights and your night vision.

q: Tuesday, 23:00, anchored in a bay with dinghies crossing to the taverna. The panel is set like this. What do you change?
a: NAV off — at anchor you show only the all-round white; sidelights say you are under way
o: Add STEAMING — a second white at the top is seen further
Leave it — in a busy bay more lights are safer
Swap ANCHOR for TRICOLOUR — it is higher and brighter
why: Rule 30: an anchored vessel shows an all-round white; sidelights and sternlight are for a vessel under way and confuse a dinghy at night.

q: Ticking off the inventory, your crew ask why the panel has a HORN button when there is an aerosol foghorn in the locker. What do you tell them?
a: The electric horn is the boat's whistle for manoeuvring and fog signals; the aerosol is the backup — test both
o: The button is for the anchor-drag alarm — the aerosol is the horn
The aerosol is for fog only; the button is for calling the marina
Either will do — a sailing yacht is not required to carry a whistle
why: A vessel over 12 m carries a whistle (Rule 33); the electric horn is it, and a can that sounds without power is the sensible spare.

q: The radar display says this and the contract forbids night sailing. The base cannot fix it this week. Do you accept the boat?
a: Yes — written on the form as unserviceable so it is not charged to you; your plan needs no radar
o: No — refuse the boat, a radar on the list must work
Yes, but only after they fit a working scanner, whatever it takes
Yes, and say nothing — an unused radar is not your problem
why: Weigh a dead item against your plan: no night or fog passages, so radar is not needed — but it goes on the form, or the check-out charges it to you.
ref: Check-in: radar and defects on the form

q: Your crew plot the plotter's position on the paper chart and it lands 100 m inland. Reading the chart's title block you find this. What is going on?
a: The chart is on another datum — apply the printed shift to GPS positions, or set the plotter to the chart's datum
o: The GPS is 100 m out — normal for a charter plotter
The chart is old and the coast has been built out since
The plotter's position offset is wrong — reset it to zero
why: GPS positions are WGS84; an older chart on ED50 needs the shift printed in its title block before a GPS position goes on it.

q: Thursday, 07:00, anchored in a bay with no phone signal and a hard sky to the north. How do you get a forecast before deciding to move?
a: Keep 16 on for the coastguard's announcement, listen on the channel the briefing gave, and ask the base on 72
o: Motor towards the base until the phone finds a signal, then open the app
Go by the barometer — a Med summer has no fronts to speak of
Call the coastguard on 16 and ask them to read you the forecast
why: Coast stations announce their weather broadcasts on 16 and read them on a working channel; the base knows the local pattern. Both are on the VHF.

fig.title: Briefing — forecast sources
lines: Coastguard weather: announced on 16, read on a working channel
No phone signal in the northern bays

q: You take the hand-bearing compass from the drawer and try it on the way out of the harbour, as shown. What does it tell you?
a: Use it well away from the binnacle and the winches — at the bow it agrees with the steering compass
o: The steering compass is 11° out — ask for it to be swung
Take bearings from the plotter's cursor from now on
Average the two readings and use 098° for the week
why: A hand-bearing compass has no deviation card: it is read where there is no iron or magnet — the bow, the pushpit — never beside the wheel.

fig.title: Hand-bearing compass — harbour mole
lines: Steering compass, bow on the mole: 093°

q: On the 42 ft catamaran the technician briefs the instruments at the starboard helm and heads for the galley. What do you ask?
a: Which readouts repeat at the port helm — you will steer from there when the quay is to port
o: Whether the two helms can run the plotter at the same time
Nothing — a catamaran is steered the same from either side
Whether the port wheel can be locked for the week
why: On a cat you moor from the helm nearest the quay; if depth, engine revs and the pilot's Standby are only to starboard, you need to know it now.

fig.title: 42 ft catamaran — helms
lines: Starboard: plotter, pilot, depth, both tachos

q: Reading the plotter's set-up page on Sunday morning you find this, left by the last crew. What do you change?
a: Distance to nautical miles and speed to knots — the chart, the log and the forecast all use them
o: Nothing — kilometres are more precise than miles
Position to decimal degrees, to match the phone app
Depth to feet, to match the depth sounder's display
why: One mile is one minute of latitude on the chart; km on the plotter and miles on the chart is how distances get doubled or halved.

q: Tuesday, in a bay, your crew mark 'the good spot for tomorrow' by pressing the plotter's MOB key. What do you do?
a: Clear it and explain: MOB starts a man-overboard display, on some sets an alert; a spot is a normal waypoint
o: Leave it — a waypoint is a waypoint, whatever key put it there
Rename it to “anchor spot” in the waypoint list and keep it
Press MOB again — the second press turns it into a waypoint
why: The MOB key is for one thing; a plotter left in MOB mode steers back to a false casualty and, with DSC linked, can send an alert.

q: Tuesday afternoon, under way, the VHF shrieks and shows this. What do you do?
a: Silence it, listen on 16 and note the position; call the coastguard if nobody answers and you can help
o: Press Acknowledge — it stops the alert for everybody at once
Switch the set off — the alarm resets itself on power-up
Send your own distress relay at once on DSC
why: A received alert is answered by the coast station; a yacht listens on 16, logs the position and acts only if nobody else does.

q: Thursday, 11:00, 24 miles from the base, the displays show this and the base closes at 18:00. When do you arrive, and what do you do?
a: About 17:00 — plan by SOG, six hours at 4 kn; call the base now and say so
o: About 15:00 — the log gives the speed, four hours at 6 kn
About 13:00 — allow for the current easing as you go
No way to tell — the current changes every hour
why: Time to go is distance over speed over the ground: 24 M / 4 kn = 6 h. Tell the base early — a late boat is a late check-out.
